doc.title: Evan Christopher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 1, 2009

chapter: Jazz, Lincoln Center and the music market
title: Lincoln Center, jazz as high art and the arts' role in community
summary: Asked about elevating jazz toward classical music, he calls it a double-edged sword. He argues musicians should serve audiences and youth, and the Lincoln Center framing can be condescending.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: Yeah. I’m going to ask you one more question that we can dub in. I’m expecting our tape to run out. I forget the circumstances, it might have been in one of the classes yesterday, you were talking about Lincoln Center and sort of this striving to make jazz, to bring it up to the level of how people think about classical music. And I’m wondering if that’s sort of a fool’s errand, because the musics are not the same — I can’t even finish my question.

I think it’s a double edged sword to try to — look we’re in the period where there’s a level of alienation from the arts in general that’s high enough that I don’t think we need to make it worse by re-framing jazz or by continuing this track of framing it as a higher art. I mean I think all of it needs to be brought down through education, that’s how I would do it, to a level where the function of the music is not only more evident but viewed as essential. I think it’s not only jazz that needs to be returned to its place, but I think more of an effort needs to done with all the different types of musics and art: classical music, opera, I think we’d need to really be serious about how we — what strategies we can recognize in the music. And in jazz the strategies are much more evident. The strategies about how we solve problems creatively and how we express our individuality in the service of community and how certain vertical disciplines of getting better at the craft have to resonate also with horizontal movement, meaning the circle has to be spreading out and the potency of the music has to be in its — not only in its expressive potentialities but in its potential to engage, to inspire. It just needs to be brought down to a vaguely more human level that I don’t think you achieve when you try to put it in the same category of musics that are already only for the most part viewed as

obligatory cultural experiences. But I think classical music needs to kind of have the same battle. I think especially when the economy is like this. You can’t continue to kind of act like the audience’s concerns aren’t important in a way, as if what you’re doing is so important that oh, they’ll come when they figure it out. You know I think we need to equally present ourselves as artists. Not just jazz, but I think we need to put ourselves on doorsteps for people and say here we are. Like we can help you. This music is here to help you. It’s here to heal you. It’s here to — we can say, we’re here to serve in a way. And to our kids, to our youth. I think all the musicians, no matter what style you’re playing: jazz, classical, or anything, I think as artists we need to be saying come check this out. Don’t mess with that over there. That will kill you. I’ve got something that you’ll like. I mean we can save some lives with this. Taking away these outlets for them to express themselves, for them to understand their own community, for them to foster respect for other individuals, for them to foster respect for themselves. You take away the arts and you’ve eliminated some very important avenues in which those things can happen. So yeah, there’s a definite problem. And here’s the contradiction. Even if end, even if you have those kids saying, “Wow, that is kind of cool” and then you want them to go to Lincoln Center for a concert, there’s a bit of a disparity. I mean that’s not their audience. That’s not my audience. I’ve been to Dizzy’s Club a couple of times, and I’ve been to a couple of Lincoln Center concerts and I’ve been to a couple of concerts on the road, but just look around. Really? And it’s not that I’m saying people aren’t getting anything out of the experience. I’m not saying that they’re only going there as a, what do they call it, some type of cultural experience that they have to do to feel like yes I support the arts and I’m cultured. Or even in a more condescending way. “I support jazz. Some of my best friends are black.” It’s that level of condescension in a way. And either way it’s completely, it’s antithetical to the true jazz experience. The true jazz experience embraces the primacy of the moment. It doesn’t make presumptions about its importance before the fact really. If it does, wow, I don’t have those kind of balls. You know? So I’m not sure how I feel about it. Economically, as a musician, it’s made things very difficult. It’s created this sense, for booking agents, there’s this top tier and there’s this top tier and there’s this price range for like Lincoln Center, and then there’s this low tier for cats like me, where the best we can expect is a few hundreds of dollars for an engagement. And there’s not a whole lot in between. There’s not a whole lot in between. And I think that’s one of the effects that this has had, just from the marketing, from the standpoint of the marketing of the music.
